title: Lotus: Learning to Understand Time-series by Learning to Forecast
summary: Time-series language models typically align numerical signals with language using labels, captions, or question-answer pairs. Although such supervision encourages linguistic representations, it does not explicitly require them to preserve information about how the underlying time-series signal evolves. We introduce forecast grounding, a pretraining principle that requires language-aligned time-series representations to remain predictive of the future evolution before they are adapted to downstream tasks. We instantiate this principle in LOTUS, which divides each time-series channel into non-overlapping patches and maps them into the LLM embedding space. It then predicts the next patch from the LLM hidden states of the time-series tokens, encouraging the learned representation to retain temporal information. To capture both temporal changes and periodic patterns, we also propose a temporal-spectral patch representation that combines each raw time-series patch with its spectral representation before mapping it into the LLM embedding space. Across three language model backbones and six downstream evaluation datasets, LOTUS achieves the best average performance with minimal trainable parameters, reaching 59.91% accuracy and outperforming the strongest matched baseline by 3.36%. Our representation analyses further show that LOTUS uses the numerical input and preserves temporal structure in its learned patch representations. These results establish forecast grounding as a promising pretraining principle, enabling compact time-series language models to outperform models 25 to 50 times their size on TSRBench.

title: Inverse Reasoning Models for Efficient Post-Training and Verification from Answer-Only Data
comments: Published at the COLM 2026 Workshop on Efficient Reasoning
summary: Post-training reasoning LLMs often requires making a tradeoff between costly supervision and compute inefficiency: supervised finetuning typically requires reasoning traces, which is data inefficient since in many applications one only has prompt-answer tuples and lacks the groundtruth chain-of-thought (CoT) sequence. On the other hand, reinforcement learning (with verifiable rewards, for example) can operate without CoT data but it is much more compute-inefficient since it requires multiple autoregressive completions per optimization step, none of which are guaranteed to give a non-zero policy gradient. In this work we explore a middleground, a self-distillation technique that uses answer-only data, treating CoT as latent variables. This relies on training a partner ``inverse reasoning LLM" that generates the original's reasoning traces conditioned on the answer. The inverse model is trained once and reused across incoming batches of answer-only data, with all generation happening offline and up front, making the approach particularly suited to continual post-training. Using Qwen3-0.6B on the Countdown and GSM8K tasks, we show that after GRPO training has saturated, a single offline distillation round from the inverse model roughly doubles pass@1 on hard prompts and, on Countdown, outperforms rejection-sampling self-distillation on every hard-tail metric at every mix ratio (with smaller gains on GSM8K); rejection sampling by construction has no signal on problems the model never solves on its own. Continued GRPO on the fresh data retains an edge at hard pass@1 but trails distillation at pass@8 and pass@32 while regenerating rollouts at every step. As an added bonus we see that the inverse model has a second application as an accurate verifier of correctness. When used for best-of-$n$ selection at test time, it raises selection accuracy on Countdown from 0.753 (majority voting) to 0.969.
comment: Published at the COLM 2026 Workshop on Efficient Reasoning

title: Do Vision CIL Methods Transfer to Protein? A Diagnostic Benchmark of Frozen Protein Encoders
comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Continual Learning for Foundation Models and Agents (CL4FM Agents)
summary: Protein function annotation operates over an expanding label space, making class-incremental learning (CIL) a natural framework for incorporating newly discovered functions without full retraining. Yet existing CIL methods have been developed largely in vision and have not been systematically evaluated over frozen protein representations. We conduct a controlled benchmark of nine representative CIL methods across five sequence-, structure-, and sequence--structure-based protein encoders and two enzyme function datasets at different scales, while keeping the encoders frozen and evaluation settings consistent across representations. We find that no method transfers reliably across encoders, and that these failures persist across alternative phase constructions. Diagnostic analyses reveal that this instability arises from weak gradient-based stability signals, substantial heterogeneity in embedding geometry, and covariance assumptions whose appropriate capacity changes with both dataset scale and encoder. These findings suggest that the representation itself should be treated as a central component of continual-learning design rather than a passive feature extractor. More generally, reliable protein CIL will require encoder-aware methods that adapt their statistical assumptions and capacity to the geometry of the representation on which they operate. Code is available at https://github.com/zygao930/ProteinCIL.
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Continual Learning for Foundation Models and Agents (CL4FM Agents)

title: Do Perturbation Predictors Learn Gene Interactions? Diagnosing Extrapolation in Agentic Screening
comments: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop ML4Molecules: Agentic Systems for Molecular Sciences
summary: High-throughput perturbation screens increasingly use machine-learning models to predict the effects of gene combinations that were never measured. A difficult case arises when both genes in a test pair were seen individually during training, but their combination was not. In this setting, standard OOD methods often fail because neither gene appears unfamiliar on its own. We therefore compare each model prediction with a simple additive prediction obtained by summing the two observed single-gene effects. The difference between them, which we call additive disagreement (AD), measures how much extra interaction effect the model introduces for an unseen combination. Across eight prediction methods and three Perturb-seq datasets, specialised neural predictors do not consistently outperform this simple additive baseline. More importantly, predictions with larger deviations from the additive baseline tend to have larger errors. Conventional output-based and embedding-based confidence signals are inconsistent across datasets and models, whereas AD remains informative across all evaluated compositional settings. We further study how this signal can guide decisions in an agentic perturbation-screening workflow. The code is available at https://github.com/zygao930/OOD.
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop ML4Molecules: Agentic Systems for Molecular Sciences

title: Following the Flow the Law Requires: Training Voice Agents to Transfer to Unseen Regulated Procedures in Debt Collection
summary: Voice agents built on large language models (LLMs) now handle customer calls, but in regulated applications completing the task is not enough: the agent must follow a conversational flow set by law. In debt collection, it must confirm it is speaking to the debtor before mentioning the debt, identify itself and the creditor, state the amount, and avoid prohibited language. Every creditor turns these rules into its own procedure and revises it. We ask whether a small, self-hosted policy can be trained once and then follow regulated procedures it has never seen. One machine-readable specification per deployment, FlowSpec, generates the policy instruction, gates the tools, supplies the supervision and defines the tests; the agent speaks only approved catalogue sentences. We fine-tune a 9-billion-parameter model on 2,506 conversations from 297 randomized procedures and evaluate a Thai outbound-call agent on four unseen deployment procedures (three debt collection, one non-debt), one from a wholly withheld lineage. Documented checks, fixed by the procedure, rise from 67--71 percents to 93--100 percents, while grounded checks, fixed by the conversation, already pass at 97--100 percents before training; scenario pass rate rises from 15/43 to 40/43. An audit of the shared specification finds 11 defects, 3 of which its own metric did not expose.

title: Token Utility for On-Policy Distillation via Local Trust-Region Optimization
comments: 10 pages, Accepted to Pre-to-Post workshop at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Token-selection methods for on-policy distillation (OPD) prioritize student-visited positions using diverse signals, including uncertainty, teacher-student disagreement, and mismatch direction. We instead derive token importance from the distillation objective itself: how much can each position's loss decrease under an equal local KL budget on the student's predictive distribution? The answer is the utility $s_t=g_t^\top F_t^\dagger g_t$, where $g_t$ is the logit gradient and $F_t$ is the categorical Fisher matrix. For reverse-KL it equals the student-weighted variance of the student-teacher log-probability ratio, and for forward-KL it equals the Pearson $χ^2$ divergence, so the appropriate utility follows from the choice of objective. On shared training checkpoints, several independently motivated criteria, including student entropy, KL disagreement, and TIP, concentrate their importance on nearly the same positions as the derived utility at a 50\% selection fraction, while diverging at stricter fractions and for direction-specific criteria. We instantiate the utility as Fisher Utility Weighting (FUW), a continuous, mean-normalized token weighting. Across seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks and three Qwen3 student-teacher pairs, FUW improves over matched uniform OPD under both reverse-KL (1.35-4.0 macro points) and forward-KL (1.08-2.71 macro points), and is competitive with existing selective methods using a single closed-form score derived from the training objective.
comment: 10 pages, Accepted to Pre-to-Post workshop at NeurIPS 2026

title: AI-Driven, Timing-Aware Power Optimization
summary: Post-route power recovery changes cell choices under tightly coupled timing, electrical and physical constraints, and the value of each change depends on what it costs to repair its side effects. We propose an AI-driven framework in which a learned model drives both phases of the optimization: it ranks the powerrecovery edits to try and the repair actions that follow, while deterministic electronic design automation (EDA) analyses govern every acceptance. The framework records baseline constraint margins, identifies the damage a recovery transaction introduces in each analysis view, holds pre-existing violations at their baseline rather than working them inside the power step, and caps repair spending at a fraction of the measured saving. An ensemble of gradient-boosted models predicts power change, normalized damage reduction and constraint-regression risk from action and timing-context features available before each trial; calibrated, conservative estimates feed separate acquisition scores for recovery and repair, with a deterministic fallback when the model is uncertain. Recovery and repair remain speculative until physical implementation and fresh analysis establish baseline preservation and positive net saving. We specify the contract, the learned policy, the transactional flow and a pre-registered public evaluation protocol on open designs. Evidence from a companion study on public designs supports the contract; the learned policy is proposed, and no trained-model results or proprietary design measurements are reported.

title: From Prompts to Silicon: Scaling LLM-Assisted Chip Design with the AI Hardware Design League
summary: The semiconductor workforce shortage has renewed interest in making chip design accessible to students without conventional very-large-scale integration (VLSI) training. We present the AI Hardware Design League (AI-HDL), an international, project-based competition in which students use Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate and iteratively refine Verilog while simulation, synthesis, timing analysis, security review, and physical verification provide the engineering feedback needed to validate the result. Across two annual cycles, AI-HDL grew from 172 to 604 participants and from 40 to 108 teams, reaching 30 universities, six community colleges, and 19 countries. In the 2026 cohort, 68.7% of participants reported no prior Verilog experience. Twenty-two teams completed the four design phases and reached final evaluation. Two division-winning designs completed physical sign-off in the SkyWater 130 nm (Sky130) process, passing design-rule checking and layout-versus-schematic verification with zero violations before being submitted for fabrication. These results show that an LLM-assisted, tool-grounded workflow can be deployed at substantial scale while also revealing that completion, rather than initial access, remains the principal challenge. AI-HDL materials and finalist artifacts are released to support replication and future study.

title: A Factor-Two Lower Bound for Complementing Two-Way Deterministic Finite Automata
summary: For every $n\ge22$, we construct a language over a fixed three-letter alphabet whose two-way deterministic state complexity is $n$ and whose complement has state complexity $2n$. Acceptance is at the left endmarker, and infinite computations reject. The lower bound holds for arbitrary deterministic recognizers. The proof uses the group of transformations induced by the witness to constrain the behavior of a smaller recognizer, then derives a contradiction from a permutation query problem. A matching halting complement follows from a $2n$-state construction for sources whose destination states determine the direction of each transition. Splitting states by incoming direction gives a $2n+2b$ upper bound for general sources, where $b$ counts states entered in both directions. In the acceptance-anywhere model of Geffert, Mereghetti, and Pighizzini, the same family has exact complexities $N$ and $2N-1$ for every $N\ge23$.

title: Thompson Sampling for Learning in Zero-Sum Games
summary: Thompson sampling (TS) achieves logarithmic and asymptotically optimal regret in classical stochastic bandits, but its behavior in multi-agent learning remains less understood. We study TS in an unknown finite two-player zero-sum matrix game with Gaussian bandit feedback. Under centralized self-play, TS samples a single payoff matrix from the posterior and plays a Nash equilibrium of the sampled game. For every fixed zero-sum game with a unique Nash equilibrium, we show that the expected cumulative duality gap is $O(\sqrt T)$. The rate improves to $O(\log T)$ for pure equilibria. We then identify the exact coefficient of the $\sqrt T$ term, which depends only on the equilibrium strategies and the noise level. We also establish a minimax lower bound matching the square-root dependence on $T$ and an instance-dependent lower bound matching the logarithmic dependence on $T$ for a class of games with a unique pure equilibrium. Experiments support the predicted rates and coefficient.

title: Stabilizer entropy cones as self-dual slices of linear rank cones: a five-party gap and dependence on the local dimension
comments: 29 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables. Data, certificates and code: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23303466. Submitted to PRX Quantum
summary: Entanglement entropies of multipartite pure states satisfy linear inequalities; for stabilizer states, the backbone of quantum error correction, the achievable entropy vectors generate a convex cone. We show that, after a linear lift, the closure of this cone is exactly the self-dual slice of a classical object on one more element than there are parties: the closed cone generated by the rank functions of arrangements of subspaces over $\mathrm{GF}(d)$ for a prime local dimension $d$, and of subgroups of abelian groups of exponent dividing $d$ in general. This correspondence brings two features of rank inequalities into play. First, the purifier acts as an extra variable: already for five parties the stabilizer cone is strictly smaller than the quantum linear rank cone, with which earlier evidence suggested it might coincide; an explicit six-variable inequality witnesses the gap. Second, the characteristic of the field enters, so the cone depends on the local dimension. It does not for up to four parties. With enough parties, the cone of $\mathbb{Z}_d$ qudits is contained in that of $\mathbb{Z}_{d'}$ qudits if and only if $d$ divides $d'$, and already for six parties the logical zero state of Steane's code lies outside the stabilizer cone of every odd local dimension. For this last result we show that the seven-variable characteristic-dependent inequalities we checked all follow from Shannon inequalities on the self-dual slice, and instead transfer one of them through a family of subgroups derived from the Fano plane.
